[ UNCLASSIFIED · RECEIVE-ONLY · YOUR OWN PERIMETER · FOR TRAINING ]

Six Engineering Projects That
See Everything Coming
Night vision, a heads-up display, a sentry tower, an RF station, a mesh
network, and a command map that fuses them all — six builds that stack into a
personal situational-awareness system, the same architecture the new defense-
tech companies are built on. Sense, connect, display, decide. Every one a
sensor, a network, or a screen.

01
Digital Night-Vision Monocular  See in total darkness with a camera that
watches infrared — and an illuminator nobody else can see

02
AR Heads-Up Display Goggles  A see-through display that floats heading,
waypoints, and teammate positions in front of your eye

03
Autonomous Sentry Tower  A tower that spots motion, slews to it, and
tracks it across the yard — a perimeter that watches on its own

04
RF Ground Station  A fixed station that watches the whole radio spectrum,
decodes what's public, and flags anything new

05
Mesh Field Radio  Pocket radios that form their own network — text and
position sharing with no cell towers at all

06
Command Map (Common Operating Picture)  One map that fuses every sensor
you built — tracks, alerts, and teammates in a single live picture
SENSORS 06 · TRACKS 03 · ALERTS 01 · MESH 3 NODES · RX ONLY

see everything coming — a Build List field guide
1 / 18

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand silicon sensor spectral response (why cameras see near-IR), active versus
passive illumination, IR illuminator design and safety, low-light imaging trade-offs (gain,
exposure, noise), and packaging optics — the foundations of electro-optical engineering.
→ the job this maps to: electro-optical (EO/IR) and imaging-systems engineering — night-vision,
surveillance-camera, and imaging-sensor teams.

!
YOUR OWN DARK, NOT SOMEONE ELSE'S
Night vision lets you see people who can’t see you. Use it on your own property, on hikes,
for wildlife, for astronomy — never to watch people who don’t know you’re there. And keep
illuminators to low-power IR LEDs: high-power IR lasers or arrays can injure eyes precisely
because you can’t see them.
NODE 01 · ONLINE

[ P R O J E C T 0 1 ]
Digital Night-Vision Monocular
See in total darkness with a camera that watches infrared — and an
illuminator nobody else can see

$60
beginner
1 weekend
// why this matters
Night vision is the original force multiplier: the side that can see in the dark owns the night.
Real image-intensifier tubes cost thousands, but a digital version is astonishingly cheap — a
camera with its infrared filter removed sees near-IR light your eyes cannot, and an IR illuminator
floods the scene with light that is invisible to everyone but your sensor. Build it into a
monocular with a small display and you can walk through a pitch-black room, read a sign at
30 metres, and watch wildlife that has no idea it is lit. It is a beginner build with a jaw-
dropping demo, and it teaches the sensor and optics fundamentals behind every EO/IR system.

Silicon sees infrared: A camera’s silicon sensor is sensitive well past visible red into near-
infrared (about 700–1000 nm); manufacturers add an IR-cut filter so daylight colours look
right. Remove it (a “NoIR” camera) and the sensor sees IR.
Active illumination: In true darkness there is little IR to see, so you add your own: an array
of 850 nm IR LEDs floods the scene with light invisible to human eyes (a faint red glow at
most) but bright to the sensor. That is active night vision.
Passive vs active: Image intensifiers amplify faint ambient light (passive, no emission);
thermal cameras see heat. Digital IR-illuminated night vision is active — cheap and effective,
but the illuminator can be seen by other IR cameras.
Low-light imaging: Higher sensor gain and longer exposure pull more from the dark at the cost
of noise and motion blur; a fast lens gathers more light. Balancing gain, exposure, and
illuminator power is the core tuning.
The monocular: A small display behind an eyepiece lens shows the live IR video, and everything
mounts in a tube with the camera and illuminator forward — a self-contained device you hold to
your eye.

// build steps
// interview questions
Get IR video
Connect the NoIR camera to the Pi and view video. Point a TV remote at it and see its LED
flash bright — proof the sensor sees IR.
Add the illuminator
Mount the 850 nm LED board next to the lens and turn the lights off. Watch the room appear
on screen while it stays pitch black to your eyes.
Tune for the dark
Adjust gain, exposure, and frame rate for the best image in true darkness. Note the trade-
off between brightness, noise, and blur.
Build the monocular
Mount camera, illuminator, display, eyepiece lens, and battery in a printed tube so you can
hold it to your eye. Add a power switch and an illuminator dimmer.
Field test
Take it outside at night. Read a sign at distance, find the range limit of your illuminator,
and watch wildlife. Film the demo — then explain why the illuminator is visible to other
cameras.

4 / 18

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand optical see-through display design (beam splitters, collimation, eye relief),
heading and position sensing (IMU + magnetometer + GPS), rendering a stable HUD from sensor
data, and designing information for a glanceable display — the core of AR/HUD and wearable-
systems engineering.
→ the job this maps to: AR / HUD, wearable-systems, and human-machine-interface engineering —
defense-headset, avionics-HUD, and AR-hardware teams.

!
EYES FIRST
A display inches from your eye must be dim enough and properly focused through a collimating
lens, and it must never be worn while driving, cycling, or in traffic. Keep most of the
field of view clear: a HUD is an aid, not a replacement for looking.
NODE 02 · ONLINE

[ P R O J E C T 0 2 ]
AR Heads-Up Display Goggles
A see-through display that floats heading, waypoints, and teammate
positions in front of your eye

$70
advanced
2 weekends
// why this matters
The most talked-about piece of modern soldier equipment is the augmented-reality headset: a see-
through display that overlays a compass, waypoints, teammate locations, and sensor alerts onto the
real world, so the wearer never looks down at a map. You can build the core of one. A small bright
display reflected off a half-mirror in front of your eye gives you a see-through HUD; an IMU
compass and a GPS feed it heading and position; a radio brings in teammate positions and alerts.
Turn your head and the bearing to the waypoint slides across your view. It is optics, embedded
systems, and UI design in one build, and the first-person footage is unlike anything else in this
series.

The optical combiner: A small bright display is reflected off a half-silvered mirror (a beam
splitter) angled in front of the eye. The mirror passes the real scene and reflects the
display, so the graphics appear overlaid on the world.
Focus and eye relief: A collimating lens between the display and the combiner sets the image’s
virtual distance so it is sharp alongside distant objects. Eye relief and combiner size set
your usable field of view.
Heading and position: An IMU with a magnetometer gives head heading (fused for stability); a
GPS module gives position. From these you compute the bearing and distance to any waypoint or
teammate.
Rendering the HUD: A microcontroller draws a compass tape, a waypoint marker at its relative
bearing, distance, and alert icons — high-contrast, minimal graphics that read at a glance
without cluttering the view.
Bringing in the team: A radio (your mesh node from project 5, or Bluetooth from a phone)
supplies teammate positions and sensor alerts from the sentry or RF station, so the HUD shows
the whole picture.
Why a half-mirror combiner instead of a screen you look at? A HUD only works if the information
sits on the world — you must see through it. A beam splitter reflects the display into your eye
while passing the real scene, so the overlay floats in front of you. A solid screen would block
the view, which defeats the purpose.
Why does the display need a collimating lens? Your eye cannot focus on a screen two inches
away. A lens between display and combiner places the image at a comfortable virtual distance,
near infinity, so the overlay and the distant world are in focus together. Without it the HUD
is a blur.
Why fuse heading instead of using the magnetometer alone? A magnetometer alone is noisy and
lags, so a compass overlay would jitter and swim as you turn your head. Fusing the gyro (fast,
but drifts) with the magnetometer (slow, but absolute) yields a smooth, stable heading —
essential for a HUD that has to feel locked to the world.

// build steps
// interview questions
Prove the optics
Mount the display, lens, and half-mirror on a bench and look through: adjust distances until
the display image is sharp while you focus on the far wall. This is the hardest step — nail
it first.
Draw a compass
Fuse IMU and magnetometer for heading and render a compass tape on the display. Turn your
head and confirm the tape scrolls smoothly and settles on north.
Add waypoints
Read GPS, define a waypoint, and draw a marker at its relative bearing with distance. Walk
toward it and watch the marker move and the distance drop.
Build the goggle
Mount everything on a 3D-printed frame or a pair of safety glasses, with the combiner in
front of one eye and the battery and MCU on the strap. Balance and secure it.
Connect the picture
Feed teammate positions and alerts in over radio and render them. Film first-person through
the combiner — the shot that shows what a HUD really is.

7 / 18

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand layered detection (a cheap trigger plus camera confirmation), object
classification on the edge, pan-tilt tracking control (visual servoing), event logging and
alerting, and designing an unattended system that runs reliably. That is the core of
autonomous-surveillance and perimeter-security engineering.
→ the job this maps to: autonomous-sensor and perimeter-security engineering — sentry-tower,
security-camera, and base-security systems teams.

!
WATCH YOUR OWN GROUND ONLY
This is a sensor tower, never a weapon: nothing gets mounted on it that can harm, ever.
Point it only at property you own or control, don’t record neighbours, public spaces, or
people who haven’t consented, and store footage responsibly. A tower that watches your yard
is a security camera; a tower aimed at others is surveillance.
NODE 03 · ONLINE

[ P R O J E C T 0 3 ]
Autonomous Sentry Tower
A tower that spots motion, slews to it, and tracks it across the yard
— a perimeter that watches on its own

$90
advanced
2 weekends
// why this matters
The modern border and base perimeter is watched by autonomous sensor towers: they detect motion,
classify what it is, slew a camera to track it, and alert an operator — no human staring at a
screen. Build a small one: a pan-tilt camera head on a mast, a wide-field motion trigger, a person
/ vehicle classifier, a tracking loop that keeps the target centred, and an alert with a snapshot
to your phone (or your command map in project 6). Watch it wake up, turn, and follow you across
the yard. It is perception, control, and systems integration — and, because it only watches,
entirely a sensor.

Cheap trigger, smart confirm: Running a camera classifier constantly is expensive. A PIR or
microwave-radar sensor with a wide field cheaply detects motion, and only then does the camera
wake, look, and classify. Layered detection is how real towers stay efficient.
Classification on the edge: A lightweight neural network (a MobileNet-class model on a Pi, or
with a Coral accelerator) distinguishes person, vehicle, and animal — so the tower ignores the
neighbour’s cat and alerts on a person.
Tracking (visual servoing): Once a target is classified, the pan-tilt head steers to keep it
centred using the same control loop as a tracking robot — pixel offset in, servo velocity out —
so the target stays in frame as it moves.
Alerting and logging: Each event gets a timestamp, class, snapshot, and track, sent to your
phone (or the command map) and logged. A good sentry is a good record keeper.
Running unattended: Weatherproofing, power (solar plus battery), watchdogs, and failure
handling are half the engineering — a sentry that dies at 3 a.m. is useless. Reliability is the
discipline.

// build steps
// interview questions
Build the head
Assemble the pan-tilt bracket with the camera, drive both axes from the Pi, and confirm full
sweep and smooth motion.
Add the trigger
Mount the PIR / radar sensor with a wide field. Have motion wake the camera and grab a
frame; log each trigger.
Classify
Run a person / vehicle / animal classifier on the triggered frame. Tune it so a person is
reliably detected and animals are ignored (or logged separately).
Track
When a person is confirmed, close the loop: compute the pixel offset from centre and drive
the pan-tilt to follow. Walk across the yard and watch it track you.
Deploy and alert
Mount it on the mast in a weatherproof box, add alerts with snapshots to your phone (or the
command map), power it, and let it run overnight. Review the log in the morning.

see everything coming — a Build List field guide
10 / 18

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand wideband spectrum monitoring, automated sweeping and logging, signal and
change detection (“new emitter”), decoding standard public protocols, antenna and station
design, and building a reliable always-on receiver. Spectrum awareness is core to EW,
SIGINT, and spectrum-management roles.
→ the job this maps to: spectrum-monitoring, SIGINT, and electronic-warfare engineering —
spectrum-management, defense-RF, and monitoring-system teams.

!
PUBLIC SIGNALS ONLY
Receive-only, and decode only signals meant to be public — ADS-B, AIS, weather satellites,
broadcast, unencrypted telemetry. Intercepting or decoding private communications (phones,
private voice, anything not broadcast to the public) is illegal in most countries. Watch the
spectrum; don’t listen to people.
// how it works
NODE 04 · ONLINE
Sweeping the spectrum: An SDR retunes across the bands in steps, capturing a power spectrum at
each; stitched together it is a wideband survey. Repeated continuously, it becomes a time-lapse
of the radio environment.
Baseline and change detection: Log the average power per frequency over days to build a
baseline; a signal where the baseline is empty is a new emitter. Flagging those is the
station’s alert function — spectrum change detection.
Decoding the public: Dedicated decoders turn broadcasts into data: ADS-B (aircraft positions),
AIS (ships), NOAA / Meteor weather images, FM and DAB. Each becomes a feed on your map.
The station: A fixed mast antenna (a discone for wideband, plus dedicated antennas), low-loss
coax, an LNA, and an SDR into a Pi running always-on software — with a waterfall dashboard you
can open from any device.
Feeding the picture: Every decoded track and every emitter alert is published to the command
map (project 6), so it shows aircraft, ships, and radio activity live around you.

[ P R O J E C T 0 4 ]
RF Ground Station
A fixed station that watches the whole radio spectrum, decodes what's
public, and flags anything new

$80
intermediate
1–2 weekends
// why this matters
A signals station doesn’t hunt one signal; it watches the whole spectrum, all the time. Build a
permanent RF ground station: an SDR on a mast antenna, continuously sweeping the bands, logging
what is on the air, decoding the public signals — aircraft (ADS-B), ships (AIS), weather
satellites, broadcast — and raising an alert when a new emitter appears where there was none. Its
waterfall dashboard becomes your radio picture of the area. It is the receive-only heart of a
signals post, and it feeds the command map with everything that transmits nearby.

Stand up the antenna
Mount a discone on a mast with low-loss coax and an LNA at the antenna. Confirm strong
reception across VHF / UHF on a waterfall.
Sweep and log
Run a continuous spectrum sweep and log power versus frequency versus time. View the survey
as a waterfall image over a day.
Build the baseline and alerts
Average several days of sweeps into a baseline, then flag frequencies that light up above it
— your new-emitter alert. Tune the threshold.
Add decoders
Run ADS-B and AIS decoders (and a weather-satellite receiver if you like) and confirm
aircraft and ships appear with positions.
Publish the picture
Push decoded tracks and alerts to a dashboard or the command map, box the station
weatherproof, and let it run for a week. Review what your area’s spectrum actually looks
like.

12 / 18

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand LoRa modulation and link budget, mesh routing and relaying, position sharing
and message encryption, node power management, and real-world range testing. Off-grid mesh
networking is core to tactical-comms and resilient-communications engineering.
→ the job this maps to: tactical-communications and resilient-network engineering — mesh-radio,
off-grid comms, and secure-communications teams.
// how it works

BUILD NOTE
Don’t write a mesh stack from scratch. Meshtastic-compatible ESP32 LoRa boards with GPS get
you a working encrypted mesh in an afternoon; the engineering is in antennas, placement,
range testing, and bridging the data into your HUD and command map.
NODE 05 · ONLINE
LoRa: A spread-spectrum modulation that trades data rate for range and sensitivity — kilobits
per second over kilometres at milliwatts. Perfect for text and positions, useless for video,
which is the point.
Meshing: Each node relays messages it hears, so a message hops node to node beyond any single
radio’s range. Flooding with hop limits keeps it simple; smarter routing keeps it efficient.
Position sharing: Nodes with GPS broadcast their position periodically; every node keeps a
table of teammates and their last known location — the data that draws dots on a map or a HUD.
Encryption: Messages are encrypted with a shared channel key, so the mesh is private to your
team even though anyone can receive the raw packets.
Range and power: Antenna height and gain, terrain, and transmit power set range; sleep modes
and duty cycling stretch a battery to days. Range testing is where the link budget becomes
real.

[ P R O J E C T 0 5 ]
Mesh Field Radio
Pocket radios that form their own network — text and position sharing
with no cell towers at all

$70
intermediate
1 weekend
// why this matters
When the network is down, jammed, or simply absent, teams still need to talk and know where each
other are. A LoRa mesh does exactly that: small radios that relay for each other, carrying short
encrypted messages and GPS positions across kilometres with no infrastructure. Build a set of
nodes, pair them, test range across your town, and watch teammate dots appear on a map — and on
your HUD from project 2. It is networking, RF, and embedded in one, and it is the connective
tissue of the whole situational-awareness stack.

WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand systems integration, data models for tracks and events, publish / subscribe
messaging, track-level sensor fusion, map-based UI design for decisions, and building a
reliable, replayable service. Command-and-control software is one of the fastest-growing
areas of defense engineering.
→ the job this maps to: command-and-control, systems, and defense-software engineering — mission-
software, sensor-fusion, and integration teams.

!
YOUR SENSORS, YOUR PICTURE
This fuses data from your own sensors on your own property and your own team. Don’t
aggregate other people’s data into it, and secure the server — it is a live map of your
sensors and your people.
NODE 06 · ONLINE

[ P R O J E C T 0 6 ]
Command Map (Common Operating
Picture)

One map that fuses every sensor you built — tracks, alerts, and
teammates in a single live picture

$25
advanced

// why this matters
Every sensor you have built so far is a separate window; command and control is about fusing them
into one picture. Build a common operating picture: a server that ingests the sentry tower’s
detections, the RF station’s aircraft and ship tracks and emitter alerts, and the mesh network’s
teammate positions, and renders them all on a live map with a timeline and an alert feed — the
same idea behind the software that runs modern defense operations. It is systems and software
engineering: data models, message buses, fusion, and a UI built for decisions. It is the capstone
that turns six projects into one system.

// build steps
The data model: Everything becomes a track (an object with position, class, and history) or an
event (a detection, an alert), each with a timestamp and a source. Defining that model well is
most of the work.
The message bus: Sensors publish to a broker (MQTT is the classic choice); the map subscribes
to everything. Publish / subscribe decouples sensors from the display, so you can add a sensor
without touching the map.
Fusion: When two sensors see the same thing (the sentry’s person and the mesh’s teammate at
that spot), the map correlates them into one track instead of two — track-level fusion, which
is where the picture becomes trustworthy.
The map UI: A web map draws tracks, alerts, sensor footprints, and a timeline, with filters —
designed for quick decisions, not for looking pretty. Alerts float to the top.
Reliability and history: A database stores every track and event so you can replay a night; the
service restarts itself, buffers when sensors drop, and never loses an alert. That is what
makes it operational.
Define the model
Write the track and event schemas (position, class, source, time, history). Keep them simple
and shared by every sensor.
Stand up the bus
Run an MQTT broker and have each sensor (sentry, RF station, mesh bridge) publish tracks and
events to it. Watch messages flow.
Build the map
Create the web map that subscribes and draws tracks, alerts, and sensor positions live. Add
a timeline and an alert feed.
Fuse tracks
Implement correlation so the same object seen by two sensors becomes one track and
confidence rises. Test by walking past the sentry with a mesh node in your pocket.
Store, replay, harden
Add a database, a replay mode, auto-restart, and buffering. Run the full stack overnight and
replay it in the morning — your own operating picture.

STACK · 6 / 6 ONLINE

[ W R A P ]
Situational awareness is a stack —
sense, connect, display, decide.
A night-vision monocular, a HUD goggle, a sentry tower, an RF station, a mesh network, a command
map — six builds that together are a personal situational-awareness stack, the same architecture
behind the systems modern defense runs on. Every one senses, connects, or displays; none of them
harm. The value is in the integration: optics, edge inference, control loops, spectrum monitoring,
networking, and systems software, working as one. That is what the defense-tech companies everyone
is talking about actually hire for.
// the skill ladder
Build them in order and each one hands you the technique the next one needs:
imaging →HUD optics →autonomous sensing →spectrum monitoring →mesh networking →command &
control

!
THE LINE THIS GUIDE STAYS ON
Every build here is receive-only, a sensor, a network, or a display. Nothing targets, jams,
intercepts private communications, or carries anything that can harm — and nothing ever gets
mounted on the sentry tower but a camera. Watch your own ground, decode only public signals,
respect people who haven’t consented, and follow local law. Build the picture, not the
weapon.
DO THIS
Build even one. Film it — a pitch-black room appearing on screen, a waypoint sliding across
